construction_sources.source_identification: Reuse Ontology, generalized LDRM procedure, and SysML metamodel or extension formalisms

entry_conditions.value: The legacy-reuse use cases, literature gap, practitioner evidence, and MBSE implementation objective have been established.

method_steps.branching_iteration_or_rework: Return to concept selection when a required relation cannot be represented.

method_steps.action: Transform ontology concepts and best practices into an implementation-neutral, end-to-end generalized reuse procedure.

method_steps.quality_or_exit_checks: Supplier and client data links are complete and logical sequencing is consistent.
method_steps.branching_iteration_or_rework: Iterate the process with expert feedback and input-output checks.

method_steps.decision_rules: Extend standard SysML elements and assign each custom construct the attributes needed by the metamodel and procedure.

method_steps.branching_iteration_or_rework: Revise stereotype definitions when conformance or expert review exposes a gap.

workflows.source_workflow_name_and_version: Legacy Design Reuse in MBSE (LDRM) methodology, 2021 thesis version

purpose_and_boundary.value: Support early space-mission decisions between legacy reuse and from-scratch design by defining context, assessing technical inheritance and rework, estimating program effects, and reporting a recommendation.

entry_conditions.value: Use begins in early architecting after a mission need and requirements have enough definition to identify a reuse slot and compare a candidate. The intended window is after SRR and before SDR in Phase A.

workflow_activities.action: Define the campaign or enterprise context, record its technical and nontechnical constraints, and bound the mission technical need.
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Begin after enough mission requirements and neighboring architecture are defined.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: The functional need, requirements, and architectural reuse slot are identified.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Revisit the context when requirements or campaign constraints change.

workflow_activities.action: Explore organizational records, screen available assets, and identify one or more reuse candidate elements at a comparable architectural level.
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Select candidates with comparable functions, usable design information, and nonobsolete realization paths.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Each candidate has a protected reference to source design information.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Return to the archive if no candidate remains viable.

workflow_activities.action: Prepare target and candidate model content in the form required by the LDRM metamodel and profile.
outputs: LDRM-compatible architecture, requirement, and interface content
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Transform nonstandard model views without changing the source model of record.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Required reuse slots, requirements, and interfaces can be queried and paired.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Iterate when the source model lacks a required view.

workflow_activities.action: Pair target requirements with candidate requirements and evaluate functional, performance, environmental, and design-constraint gaps.
inputs: Candidate requirements and supported derived requirements
outputs: Requirement pairs, no-match cases, gap magnitudes, and satisfaction flags
tools_and_settings: SysML requirement diagrams and custom tables
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Pair like with like. Derive an absent candidate requirement only when other model evidence supports it.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Every target requirement is paired, identified as unsupported, or marked unresolved.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Iterate when a requirement is nonmeasurable or absent from the candidate model.

workflow_activities.action: Pair target and candidate energy, information, material, and structural interfaces at the relevant decomposition level, then identify missing or incompatible interfaces.
outputs: Interface pairs, no-match cases, gap magnitudes, and satisfaction flags
tools_and_settings: SysML internal block diagrams and custom tables
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Compare endpoint roles and interface details rather than treating visual similarity as satisfaction.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Every in-scope target interface has a pair or an explicit no-match state.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Descend to a lower decomposition level when a high-level interface hides material differences.

workflow_activities.action: Classify each requirement and interface gap and determine whether the candidate is compatible without, with moderate, or with substantial modification.
outputs: Compatibility assessment and filtered compatible candidates
workflow_activities.automation: Tabulation can be automated after manual coding
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Use source-defined none, minor, major, no-similar-item, and oversatisfied gap classes.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: A candidate compatibility designation is recorded.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Exclude an incompatible candidate or retain uncertainty when evidence is insufficient.

workflow_activities.action: Propose rework actions for each nonzero requirement or interface gap and trace each action to the affected candidate element.
outputs: Rework sets and preliminary work breakdown structure
tools_and_settings: SysML Rework Action and Rework Set stereotypes
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Each action must address a named gap and affected subelement.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Every material gap has a rework action or a documented infeasibility.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: One gap may require several actions, and actions may be revised after discipline analysis.

workflow_activities.action: Use supporting discipline analyses to assess rework feasibility and effort, then identify effects on qualification, verification, and integration testing.
outputs: Feasibility, effort designation, testing impact, and refined rework set
workflow_activities.decision_rules: A rework action proceeds only when supporting analysis finds it feasible. Changed heritage items require renewed assurance.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: The rework set records action feasibility, effort, and testing or qualification impact.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Iterate for every action and every gap. Revise actions when analyses expose new constraints.

workflow_activities.action: Compile the full rework and compatibility evidence, validate that the modified candidate can meet the mission need, and issue a technical inheritance assessment.
workflow_activities.automation: Partly automated compilation with expert review
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Validate both mission-need satisfaction and the internal consistency of the technical assessment.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Reuse feasibility and a rework campaign are reported for each supported candidate.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Rank several candidates or reject all candidates when necessary.

workflow_activities.decision_rules: Run only when the model supplies the required size and cost drivers.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Comparable person-month estimates are produced for both design approaches.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: The DAILI case stops this activity because required program data are absent.

citations.quote: This work presents a remedy in the form of the Legacy Design Reuse in MBSE (LDRM) methodology. It is a systematic approach for conducting technical and programmatic analyses for informing legacy reuse decisions in the early design phases of a mission.

The first, reuse of the bus subsystems across the AeroCube 10 and DAILI CubeSat missions, demonstrates nominal procedures and outcomes for 3 of 4 subsystems explored; model incompatibilities in the attitude control system led to recommendations to the sponsor for improvements to MBSE model practices and curation.

End-to-end application of LDRM, therefore, should sequentially answer each of these questions: 1. For a given functional need in a mission of interest, are there any existing designs that merit consideration for potential reuse? Are there any that can be immediately excluded? 2. Does a reuse candidate design satisfy the functionality and constraints in the mission of interest? If not, what are the types and magnitudes of the gaps? 3. What rework actions may be required to address these gaps?

Additional value-added is delivered by the methodology's foundation in an MBSE environment. This primarily emerges from the integrated data landscape that ensures that authoritative and up-to-date information is used throughout the analysis.

The notional user of LDRM is a systems engineer on a mission design project in the early phases of development. This engineer is tasked with trading design solutions for key functional elements of the system. The user is also experienced with MBSE methods, practices, and tools.

At the highest level, the heritage reuse process is decomposed into three central activities: 1) defining the context of the reuse decision, 2) conducting a technical inheritance process for assessing reuse feasibility, and 3) assessing the "value" of the reuse decision in terms of impacts on programmatic factors, such as cost and schedule, for the MoI.
Records campaign/enterprise vision, objectives, and constituent missions/systems; these factors may constrain the pool of potential reusable assets and the value of their redeployment.
In particular, two key indicators are compared between the RCE in its native mission and the technical need slot in the MoI: requirements and interfaces.

Evaluates the rework/adaptation effort necessary to adapt an RCE to fully satisfy the MoI Technical Need. In particular, this step is focused on bridging the gaps in requirement and interface pairs identified in Step 2.2.
An important consideration in a reuse scenario is the degree to which the RCE will impact the testing and qualification campaign of the MoI.

The last high-level step of the generalized procedure evaluates the potential impacts of the feasible reuse scenarios on the MoI in terms of programmatic estimates (i.e., cost, schedule, systems engineering effort).

The first case study is sourced from historical and ongoing development projects at The Aerospace Corporation. It places particular emphasis on the technical inheritance aspects of the LDRM methodology - we set out to demonstrate the degree to which the inheritance procedure may predict the rework effort implemented across the native and new missions.
The AeroCube Program is a coordinated effort at the Aerospace Corporation that develops, demonstrates, and evaluates the capabilities of kilogram-class spacecraft.

Further, an explicit effort was made to ensure that the models were reusable for future AeroCube missions. Reuse of this MBSE modeling effort was attempted for the DAILI mission, which is in the concluding stages of integration and testing at the time of this writing.
DAILI is tasked with measuring daytime thermospheric $ O_{2} $ densities and ionospheric densities and heights during the day and night from an ISS-like orbit.
Additionally, the day/night measurement ConOps requires that the CubeSat operate nearly constantly - a practice not common among CubeSats.
The mission is a dual-spacecraft mission, with each satellite (known as "A" and "B") being nearly identical 1.5 U spacecraft.

The mission launched in April 2019 as a secondary payload on a Cygnus resupply mission to ISS. The satellites were deployed from Cygnusmounted CubeSat dispensers into an ISS-adjacent orbit of 480 km and 51 degrees inclination.

This chapter details end-to-end development and demonstration of the LDRM methodology. First, a framework guiding each step of the development process is presented; this framework spans several layers of refinement, from a guiding ontology, to a generalized reuse procedure, and finally to implementation in an MBSE environment.

The starting point for the framework is a Reuse Ontology, whose function is to provide unambiguous definitions of relevant reuse concepts and relationships among them. This ontology, represented via a conceptual map, frames the methodology to focus on the legacy reuse question. From here, a generalized reuse procedure is defined. The concepts from the ontology are traced into this logic to define an end-to-end process from initial inputs to final deliverables. This process flow is then codified into the MBSE environment via a metamodel and a language-specific Reuse Profile.

Concepts in the ontology are those that have been explored in preceding chapters - sourced from literature, the best practices survey, and discussions with Subject Matter Experts in relevant fields. However, only those concepts with some direct influence on the logic, procedure, or implementation of legacy reuse and the methodology (itself an entry in the ontology) are included.
Additionally, in this step we also seek to incorporate the lessons learned on reuse best practices and areas for improvement from the reuse survey detailed in Chapter 3.

A metamodel, then, can be seen as an MBSE-oriented refinement of the reuse ontology discussed previously. From this metamodel, we then proceed to building the reuse-specific modeling constructs via canonical SysML formalisms.

SysML's extension mechanism (SysML itself being an extension of the Unified Modeling Language, UML) allows for users to tailor the language to suit the needs of a given modeling effort or discipline/industry.

Additionally, the constituent steps and sub-steps of the process were developed in conformance to the findings of the best practices study where respondents collectively identified critical aspects of current reuse practices and areas for improvement. Lastly, the procedure was iterated on in consultation with subject matter experts such that industry best practices and expert opinions both strongly suggest validity of the logical set of activities.
Additionally, the face validity of this claim was reinforced with feedback from experts in NASA's MBSE Community of Practice and at The Aerospace Corporation's MBSE office.

The modeling effort was proposed to the AeroCube team "as a service" - in this model, the MBSE team would parallel the efforts of the AC10 architecting team by developing a system model that would follow along-side the project.

A similar "MBSE as a service" model was adopted by the MBSE Office - an expanded modeling effort included the addition of advanced behavioral modeling, activity execution, and more detailed component definition.
